SourceActivities: 4.1 Notice and Wonder: Circles Circles Circles
Optional 4.3 extension: polygon net (original publisher figure NOT used)

Tasks.Prompt: Construct one circle centred O and six equal-radius circles centred at consecutive vertices of its inscribed regular hexagon. Record two observations/questions. Draw two distinct polygons whose vertices are circle intersections; shade them with two colours/hatchings and write two falsifiable conjectures. Mark any claim not justified by equal-radius evidence.

Criteria.Criterion: Seven-circle radius construction or correct labelled given model
Two distinct polygons built from actual intersections and differentiated by shading/hatching
Two meaningful geometric conjectures after notice/wonder
Evidence-based radius argument and explicit identification of at least one unproven visual claim

Tasks.Accept: Any distinct valid polygons, marked conjectures with coherent reasons; no fixed publisher artwork necessary
Tasks.Reject: Two copies of the same polygon, unlabelled conjectures or asserting unsupported equal lengths

Tasks.Prompt: Construct two equilateral triangles of different sizes using a regular hexagon and its centre, for example OAB and ACE. Label O,A..F, each chord and circle radius. Explain why OAB has side r and ACE has side sqrt(3)r, and why both are equilateral.

Criteria.Criterion: Nonzero centre/radius and valid regular hexagon with six consecutive vertices
Two actual equilateral triangles of distinct sizes, correctly labelled
Circle membership, equal chords / 60/120-degree central-angle justification
Mathematically correct comparison of side lengths and preservation of permitted tool moves

Tasks.Accept: Any two nondegenerate different-sized equilateral triangles with valid source-aligned construction; alternate rotations/reflections valid
Tasks.Reject: Two same-size triangles, purely visual equality claim or only numeric answers

Tasks.Prompt: Given a circle of positive radius r, construct a regular hexagon, the alternating-vertex triangle ACE and central triangle OAB. Justify each triangle's three equal sides and explain why ACE is larger.
Tasks.Expected: OAB has all sides r; ACE has equal central spans 120 degrees and chord length sqrt(3)r, greater than r for r>0.

Criteria.Criterion: Correct distinct triangles OAB and ACE
Radius and equal-chord justification for both equilateral triangles
Correct size comparison with no false publisher source claim

Items.Prompt: The two circles centred A and B each have radius AB and intersect at C. Explain why triangle ABC is equilateral.
Items.Expected: AC=AB from A circle, BC=AB from B circle, so all three equal.

Items.Prompt: In a regular hexagon A..F inscribed in radius-r circle centred O, name at least eight mathematically guaranteed equilateral triangles using O and hexagon vertices.
Items.Expected: Six central adjacent-vertex triangles OAB,OBC,OCD,ODE,OEF,OFA and the two alternating triangles ACE,BDF. Do not claim these are all possible triangles without further review.

Items.Prompt: Two radius-r circles centred A and B, with AB=r, intersect at C and D. Which must be true: AC=BC, AC=BD, CD=AB, or A-C-B-D is necessarily a square?
Items.Expected: AC=BC and AC=BD are guaranteed (each r), while CD=sqrt(3)r need not equal AB=r; the rhombus A-C-B-D is not a square.

Items.Prompt: Line CD is perpendicular to AB at AB's midpoint M. Does AB automatically bisect CD? Explain.
Items.Expected: Not necessarily: CD need not have M as its midpoint, although it is perpendicular to AB.

Items.Prompt: Given two points A and B only, can an unmarked straightedge alone construct the equidistant locus? Could a compass alone locate two equidistant points? Explain.
Items.Expected: An unmarked straightedge alone cannot determine the midpoint/locus from two isolated marked points; a compass opened to r>AB/2 and centred at A and B locates the two intersection points X,Y, each equidistant.

Items.Prompt: Take A=(−4,0), B=(4,0), M=(0,0), E=(−1,2), and perpendicular bisector x=0. Determine AM vs BM, whether E is closer to A or B, and whether EM must equal EA.
Items.Expected: AM=BM=4; EA²=13, EB²=29 and EM²=5. Thus E is closer to A and EM is not equal to EA.

Items.Prompt: If a circle centred P passes through Q and R, must PQ=PR? Explain.
Items.Expected: Yes; both are radii of the same circle.

Items.Prompt: Give ordered moves from distinct A,B to construct the rhombus A-C-B-D from two congruent circles and their intersections.
Items.Expected: Draw circles with centres A,B, common radius AB, label intersections C,D on opposite sides of AB, connect AC,CB,BD,DA.

Items.Prompt: Circle centre A radius AB contains points B and C. A different circle centred B also has radius AB and contains D. Which guaranteed distances equal AB?
Items.Expected: AB=AC=BD by appropriate circle membership; no unsupported chord equality follows.
